newsitem.title: UK: Jury out on Beckett's British competition policy.
newsitem.headline: Jury out on Beckett's British competition policy.

text.p: In the two months since taking up her post, Britain's new Trade and Industry Secretary, Margaret Beckett, has blocked a merger in the brewing industry and launched a major review of utilities regulation.
But analysts said her actions, decisive though they may be, still do not indicate a dramatic change of direction on competition and mergers under the new Labour government.

Summing up her approach so far as pragmatic rather than dogmatic, they said some of the fears that Labour could be opposed to mergers on principle have dissipated without a clear view emerging on what Beckett's guiding principles would be.
"So far, the jury is out," Nigel Hawkins, transport and utilities analyst at Yamaichi Securities, told Reuters.
"Each particular situation (so far) has been looked at on a case-by-case basis, so it's early days," he said.
"I think it is pretty difficult to see," David Campbell, a director of stockbrokers Greig Middleton, told Reuters.
"They talked clearly in the run-up to the election about being pro-competition, of the disadvantages of agglomeration and of being prescriptive on mergers," he said.
"That sort of approach seems to have disappeared."
Beckett's latest move on Monday was to announce a major review of the regulation of utilities, covering the water, gas, electricity and telecommunication sectors.
The review is intended to lead to a consultation paper by the end of the year outlining general principles to utilities regulation and any options for change.
Department of Trade and Industry officials said it was unlikely there would be any bill on utilities regulation before next year at the earliest, if it was decided one was needed.
But there will be a new competition bill this Autumn, after a broad-ranging consultation exercise, they said.
Beckett's announcement on utility regulation came three days after she blocked a merger between brewing giant Bass Plc and Carlsberg-Tetley saying it would act against the public interest.
But analysts said both the utilities sector and the brewing industry were special cases, which made it hard to extrapolate its impact for other industrial sectors.
Utilities have been a consistent target of Labour criticism and are bracing themselves for the announcement of a windfall tax on their profits after Tuesday's budget.
The brewing merger decision, although a shift from past judgments, also came against the background of debate about excessive concentration in the industry.
"Some of the significant ones (decisions) have their individual factors which make it very difficult...," said Hawkins when asked whether there was an over-riding theme.
"I think so far it's pragmatic although we're dealing with a relatively small number of cases...
"In fairness the decisions so far have been evenly balanced ...It's a little early to say whether there's consistency."

Business leaders have been heartened by Beckett's announcement last month that she would not merge the two competition regulatory bodies -- the Office of Fair Trading (OFT) and the Monopolies and Mergers Commission (MMC).
They also welcomed her decision to abandon pre-election pledges to change the burden of proof in merger cases to make companies prove they are in the public interest.
But analysts said Labour did seem to be making competition -- and the resultant benefits for the consumer -- the priority in its approach to both regulation and merger policy.
"What has been the key criteria...is what impact has it had on the consumer," said Hawkins.
But Campbell added: "It's obvious...in broad terms, that achieving mergers is likely to be more difficult than under a Tory (Conservative) administration."
